Okay, so ketosis. Normally you get energy from glucose, obtained from carbohydrates in your diet. But when you don't consume enough carbs the body instead gets energy from fat by way of glycogen. Unfortunately when the body switches from one to the other you feel crappy for about a week: fatigued, achy, etc. This is what's known as the Keto Flu. If you were on a starvation diet the body would start using up your fat stores in the exact same process.

But keto flu eventually passes, and now all of your energy is coming from fat, which means no more "high blood sugar --> insulin --> low blood sugar --> consume carbs --> repeat". This results in consistent and sustained energy levels. Additionally since insulin triggers appetite, especially appetite for more carbs, you will now eat less.

It's still a calories in/calories out game though and generally speaking if you if you consume more calories than you expend then you will still put weight on. The point is on keto it's much easier to consume less. If you weren't aware the Atkins Diet is basically a low carb diet.

Going into ketosis and maintaining it can be a struggle for some people, and if you read some of the posts on r/keto you'll see mention of other factors that can have an effect here. But you won't know until you try. I advise against buying the test strips for your urine though: They aren't cheap, they have a relatively short shelf life once opened, and most significantly you will know when you go into ketosis AKA if you're not sure then you probably aren't. The test strips are useful mostly for clinicians.

I singled out protein because there's a tendency for people to NOT want to eat more fat -- and when I say fat I mean fats and oils BUT not transfats -- because fat has been demonized for so long (as a side note there is no correlation between dietary fat and coronary disease, though do not take my word for it please do your own research on the matter). But when they switch to a low carb diet (or keto) they now need to get the calories that were from carb from something else, and since they are (incorrectly) scared of fat they increase protein instead. I forget the specifics but this is really bad for you -- in weightlifter forums you will sometimes see posts about guys who end up in the hospital for this reason. Again you should be looking for about 70% of your calories from fats and the rest from protein and carbs.

If it helps you wrap your head around it think of the traditional Inuit diet, which was basically fat (mostly) and meat. A study done in the early 1900s found the Inuits were pretty much in ketosis all of the time, and they were fine. Now they've all adopted our diet and they are much worse off for it.

As far as the protein powder goes it would depend on how much protein your consuming in total. Also unless I'm mistaken there's usually lots of sweetener in those powders, so it may actually not be appropriate for that reason. Check the label.

Reducing carbs is healthier there's no question IMO, but that doesn't mean it's a health food diet because you could still be eating a lot of highly processed foods and food additives, do you see what I mean? Generally, however, people do more food preparation when they switch to a low carb (because processed and fast foods have so many carbs) and as a result they eat healthier. But it does make it harder, for instance to find something to eat when you go out. And fast food forgetaboutit.

I could go on and on, obviously and happily so, but tht's enough to start. But if you still have more questions don't hesitate. I will mention however that another added bonus of low carb is getting HFCS out of your diet.
